COLUMBUS — A Lowndes County man has been sentenced to more than 13 years in federal prison for trafficking methamphetamine, authorities announced.

Calvin Baskin, 55, of Columbus, was sentenced to 157 months in prison after previously pleading guilty in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Mississippi. The charge stems from his arrest on Aug. 8, 2024, according to court documents.

In addition to the prison term, Baskin was ordered to serve five years of supervised release following his incarceration.

U.S. Attorney Scott F. Leary said the case reflects ongoing efforts by law enforcement to combat drug-related crime in Mississippi communities.

“Some communities here face daily violence driven by the illegal drug trade,” Leary said. “This investigation and prosecution reflect the daily vigilance exhibited by state and federal law enforcement.”

Officials said Baskin was convicted of trafficking more than 50 grams of methamphetamine.

Drug Enforcement Administration Assistant Special Agent in Charge Anessa Daniels-McCaw said the sentence underscores the seriousness of drug trafficking offenses.

“Methamphetamine trafficking brings nothing but misery and crime to our doorsteps,” Daniels-McCaw said. “This sentence reflects the gravity of the threat posed by illegal drugs and the power of interagency cooperation.”

Lowndes County Sheriff Eddie Hawkins also praised the collaboration among agencies involved in the case.

“This sentencing sends a clear message that those who traffic illegal drugs and endanger our communities will be held accountable,” Hawkins said.

The case was investigated by the Drug Enforcement Administration, the Lowndes County Sheriff’s Department, the Mississippi Bureau of Narcotics and the U.S. Marshals Service. Assistant U.S. Attorney Clyde McGee prosecuted the case.

Officials said the case is part of broader federal initiatives, including the Homeland Security Task Force and Project Safe Neighborhoods, which focus on reducing violent crime and dismantling drug trafficking organizations.

MONTICELLO — Four people were injured and two suspects are in custody following a shootout Monday morning at a Sonic Drive-In in Monticello , authorities said.

Monticello Police Chief Sterling Allen said the incident began around 10:58 a.m. April 6, when he received a call about an active shooter at the Sonic on F.E. Sellers Drive.

“As I exited the police department, I heard what no law enforcement officer ever wants to hear… gunfire,” Allen said in a statement.

Officers with the Monticello Police Department and deputies from the Lawrence County Sheriff’s Office arrived within minutes, securing the scene and rendering aid to victims. Four individuals were struck by gunfire and injured. Their conditions have not been released.

According to Monticello Mayor Justin Mullins, the shooting stemmed from an argument between groups of people that escalated into gunfire. No bystanders were reported injured.

Authorities said multiple nearby businesses were also hit by gunfire during the incident.

Two arrests have been made, and additional arrests are expected as the investigation continues, Allen said in a release posted to Facebook around 3 a.m.

Emergency responders from multiple agencies assisted at the scene, including the Monticello Fire Department, Lawrence County Volunteer Fire Department, Life Guard Ambulance Service and Med Air. A helicopter was seen landing nearby, according to witnesses.

State and federal agencies, including the Mississippi Highway Patrol and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, are also involved in the investigation.

“This remains an active and ongoing investigation,” Allen said. “I urge anyone who witnessed this incident or has information to contact the Monticello Police Department.”

Anyone with information is asked to call the department at 601-587-7732.

JACKSON — Multiple arrests have been made and several weapons seized following a targeted law enforcement operation at the Rebelwood apartments, city officials announced Tuesday, part of an ongoing effort to curb violent crime in Jackson.

Jackson Police, working with federal partners including the U.S. Marshals Service, served three arrest warrants and executed two search warrants during the April 7 operation, Police Chief Dr. RaShall Brackney said. Authorities took four people into custody and recovered four firearms, including three AR-style pistols.

Those arrested include Isaac Gibson, 26; Frederick Williams, 23; Cordarius Beasley, 23; and Annie Smith, 49. Charges range from possession of a firearm by a convicted felon to murder, with bond set between $40,000 and no bond, Brackney said.

The enforcement action follows a pattern of violent crime at the complex, including two recent homicides. Brackney identified one victim as Travarius Cooper and said the area had generated hundreds of calls for service.

“This operation has removed dangerous individuals and illegal weapons from our streets, and we are not done yet,” Brackney said. “If you bring violence into Jackson, we will find you, we will arrest you, and we will hold you accountable.”

Officials said the investigation remains ongoing, with additional warrants outstanding and more arrests possible.

Authorities described those arrested in connection with the homicide as acquaintances, but declined to provide further details about possible gang affiliations, citing the active investigation.

During the operation, officers recovered multiple firearms, which Brackney said reduces opportunities for future violence. “That means there are four less opportunities to commit homicides and violence in our community,” she said.

Mayor John Horhn said the crackdown is part of a broader strategy targeting high-crime areas across the city.

“We’re going to tackle them one by one to make sure that we send a strong message that criminal activity, particularly violent activity, is not going to be condoned in the city of Jackson,” Horhn said.

Police said they will maintain a strong presence in the Rebelwood area and continue working with federal agencies, including the DEA and ATF, to address ongoing criminal activity. Officials also urged residents to come forward with information as the investigation continues.

IUKA – A woman was sentenced Wednesday to 30 years in prison after pleading guilty to attempted murder and aggravated assault in separate Prentiss County cases, according to the First Circuit Court District attorney’s office.

District Attorney Jason D. Herring said Veronica Gillespie pleaded guilty April 8, 2026, to attempted murder in connection with an Aug. 26, 2023, incident in Prentiss County. Gillespie also pleaded guilty to one count of aggravated assault stemming from a Nov. 8, 2022, incident in the county.

After accepting the guilty pleas, Circuit Court Judge Kelly Mims sentenced Gillespie to 40 years in the custody of the Mississippi Department of Corrections on the attempted murder charge, with 10 years suspended, leaving 30 years to serve.

On the aggravated assault charge, Gillespie was sentenced to 20 years in the custody of the Mississippi Department of Corrections, with all 20 years suspended. Prosecutors said that sentence will run consecutive to the sentence imposed in the attempted murder case.

The district attorney’s office recognized Booneville Police Department Detective Karl Courtney for his work on the investigations.

The cases were prosecuted by Assistant District Attorneys Joel Baldwin and Reagan Wise on behalf of the state.

The sheriff’s department said deputies with the Narcotics Division, assisted by the SWAT Team, Criminal Investigations Division and Patrol Division, served the warrant around 5:55 a.m. April 6 at the home of Jack Ceaser, 46, and Jessica Stewart, 42, at 726 W. Lakeshore Drive.

Investigators said the warrant was the result of a lengthy investigation prompted by numerous community complaints about suspected drug trafficking at the residence.

According to authorities, Ceaser was inside the home when deputies arrived and was seen attempting to destroy evidence. He was taken into custody without incident.

A search of the residence turned up what officials described as an aggravating quantity of methamphetamine, along with plastic baggies, a digital scale and a large amount of cash.

Ceaser was taken to the Pearl River County Correctional Facility and charged with felony aggravated trafficking of a controlled substance and tampering with physical evidence.

Authorities said Stewart was not at the residence when the warrant was served. A warrant will be issued charging her with felony aggravated trafficking of a controlled substance.

Sheriff David Allison praised the work of the Narcotics Division, SWAT Team, Criminal Investigations Division and Patrol Division, and thanked community members for reporting suspected drug trafficking activity.

Anyone with narcotics tips is asked to call 601-403-2582.

Across the United States each year, Americans pause on April 9 to observe National Former Prisoner of War Recognition Day, a solemn occasion honoring service members who endured captivity in defense of the nation.

The date marks the anniversary of the Bataan Death March, one of the most harrowing episodes of World War II. On April 9, 1942, U.S. and allied forces surrendered to the Imperial Japanese Army on the Bataan Peninsula in the Philippines. In the days that followed, thousands of captured Americans were forced to march under brutal conditions, suffering abuse, starvation and death. More than 500 Americans died during the march, which was later classified as a war crime.

National Former Prisoner of War Recognition Day was established decades later through the efforts of former POWs who sought formal acknowledgment of their bravery and sacrifice. Their advocacy led to congressional action in 1988, when then-President Ronald Reagan signed a proclamation designating April 9 as a day of national recognition.

Since then, communities across the country have marked the observance with ceremonies, memorial events and the flying of the POW/MIA flag, a symbol of remembrance for those who were prisoners of war or remain missing in action.

The observance also serves as a reminder of the enduring physical and emotional toll captivity can take on service members. Former POWs have historically faced long recoveries after returning home, often carrying the lasting trauma of their imprisonment.

In a 2025 proclamation, the President called on Americans to honor former prisoners of war and recognize their sacrifices, noting that many endured captivity “as a consequence of defending American freedom.” The proclamation also urged federal, state and local officials, as well as civic organizations, to observe the day with appropriate ceremonies and activities.

National Former Prisoner of War Recognition Day remains one of the nation’s more somber military observances. It’s a day not only to reflect on the horrors of war, but also to recognize the resilience, courage and enduring spirit of those who survived captivity in service to their country.

PHILADELPHIA – A man wanted on multiple felony charges in Neshoba County is now back in custody.

According to the Neshoba County Sheriff’s Department, Reginald Triplett returned to the Neshoba County Detention Facility after his arrest out of state. Authorities took him into custody in Cleveland, Ohio, just a few weeks ago. Today, he arrived at the detention facility at approximately 2:00 p.m.

Previously, Queen City Newsfeed reported that Triplett was arrested in Ohio on March 27, 2026 . Since then, officials have worked to bring him back to Mississippi.

Officials say USTE/Global Solutions, a private prisoner transport company, handled the transfer.

Earlier, Triplett faced 18 felony charges issued through the Neshoba County Circuit Court. After his arrest by the U.S. Marshals Service in Ohio, officials arranged his return.

Meanwhile, Sheriff Eric Clark stressed that deputies will continue to track down those who try to avoid arrest.

“Anyone attempting to evade charges or avoid court will be located and returned to face justice,” Clark said. “We will use all available resources to make that happen.”

Now, Triplett remains in custody at the Neshoba County Detention Facility. He will wait there until his court proceedings begin.

As with all criminal cases, Triplett is presumed innocent until proven guilty in a court of law.

JACKSON — Jackson Police Chief Dr. RaShall Brackney will continue a series of community meetings across Jackson in April and May, inviting residents to share concerns and help shape public safety efforts citywide.

The meetings follow outreach that began in February, when Brackney met with residents, business owners and faith leaders in Wards 5 and 6 to discuss neighborhood priorities and ways the Jackson Police Department can strengthen partnerships with the community.

The next round of meetings will expand to remaining wards through a mix of evening gatherings and daytime outreach events.

Each meeting will include remarks from Brackney, an overview of current public safety initiatives and an open listening session for residents to ask questions, voice concerns and offer ideas.

“I want every neighborhood in Jackson to know that their voice matters and that their police department is listening,” Brackney said. “These meetings are a chance for me to sit down with residents where they live, worship and work, to hear directly about what’s working, what isn’t, and how we can move forward to make every part of this city safer.”

Upcoming meetings are scheduled for April 14 at the Georgetown Event Center, April 16 at Christ United Church, April 30 at Stronger Hope Church, May 1 at Union Station and May 5 at the South Jackson Community Center.

Residents are encouraged to attend the meeting in their ward or any session that fits their schedule.

OXFORD — A Memphis man has been sentenced to more than 14 years in federal prison after pleading guilty to kidnapping a woman in Southaven, authorities said.

Elmer Smith, 39, of Memphis, Tennessee, was sentenced by Senior U.S. District Court Judge Michael P. Mills to 170 months in prison, followed by three years of supervised release. He was remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service after sentencing.

According to court documents, Smith traveled from Memphis to Southaven on Feb. 15, 2024, in search of the victim, with whom he had an intimate relationship. Authorities said he located her at her workplace, assaulted her and forced her into his vehicle before taking her back to Memphis without her consent.

The victim was later located by the Memphis Police Department, which arrested Smith a short time after the abduction.

U.S. Attorney Scott F. Leary said the crime would not be tolerated.

“Such conduct is unconscionable and will not be tolerated in our district,” Leary said in a statement, adding that those who travel to Mississippi to commit crimes “will be caught, prosecuted and jailed.”

Robert Eikhoff, special agent in charge of the FBI Jackson Field Office, said the sentence sends a clear message that violent acts will be prosecuted.

“There is no excuse for the abuse or the profound trauma inflicted on the victim,” Eikhoff said, adding that the FBI will continue working with law enforcement partners to hold offenders accountable.

Authorities credited the Southaven Police Department and the Memphis Police Department for their work on the case.

The case was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Philip Levy and Robert Mims.

JACKSON — The Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks and its Mississippi Museum of Natural Science will host the annual “NatureFEST!” event April 11, offering a full day of outdoor-themed activities for visitors of all ages.

The event is scheduled from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. at the museum, located in LeFleur’s Bluff State Park. Organizers describe NatureFEST as a combination of a festival, nature outing and museum experience designed to encourage exploration and hands-on learning.

Visitors can expect live animal encounters, demonstrations, and opportunities to interact with museum scientists, along with a variety of outdoor activities throughout the day.

“NatureFEST is one of our favorite days of the year,” Museum Director Angel Rohnke said. “It is an incredible opportunity for families to connect with Mississippi’s natural world in fun, memorable ways and to see firsthand how science, conservation, and discovery all come together here at the Museum.”

Activities will include animal presentations from Wild Acres, Freedom Ranch and the Hattiesburg Zoo, fish feedings in the museum’s aquariums, and access to exhibits such as “Giants of the Ice Age.” Guests can also take part in interactive programs, watch artist Ellen Langford at work and meet author Kay Meadows.

The event will also feature plant sales from Camp Creek Native Plants, local vendors and food trucks, including Skenny Burgers, Gator’s and Mo’Betta Desserts. Food and vendor purchases are not included with admission.

Admission to NatureFEST is included with regular museum entry or a Mississippi Museum of Natural Science Foundation membership. General admission is $9 for adults, $7 for youth ages 3 to 18 and $8 for seniors ages 60 and older.

The day will begin with the Buffalo Peak Outfitters Hoka 5K Hike/Run, which requires registration and includes admission to NatureFEST.

The Mississippi Museum of Natural Science is located at 2148 Riverside Drive in Jackson and offers exhibits and programs focused on the state’s natural heritage year-round.

STARKVILLE — Starkville has earned national recognition after being voted the No. 1 Best Small Town in the South in a readers’ choice ranking by USA Today , highlighting the city’s blend of culture, hospitality, and small-town charm.

The ranking, part of USA Today’s annual 10 Best Readers’ Choice Awards, focused on towns with populations of around 25,000 or fewer. An expert panel selected nominees, and readers determined the final rankings. Starkville topped the list, praised for offering more than just a traditional college-town experience.

Located in eastern Mississippi near the Alabama state line, Starkville sits in Oktibbeha County and is part of the Golden Triangle region, which also includes Columbus and West Point. The city is about 25 miles west of the Alabama state line and roughly 125 miles northeast of Jackson, placing it in a region known for its mix of rural landscapes and growing economic development.

At the heart of Starkville is Mississippi State University, which plays a major role in shaping the city’s identity, economy and culture. But according to USA Today’s description, Starkville stands out for much more than its college roots.

The publication highlighted the city’s thriving arts scene, historic districts and access to outdoor recreation, including birdwatching opportunities and nearby outdoor areas. Among its notable attractions is the Ulysses S. Grant Presidential Library, which houses an extensive collection of artifacts and correspondence related to the former president.

Local tourism leaders also point to Starkville’s growing food scene as a major draw. The city offers a range of dining options, from farm-to-table cuisine and Southern specialties to international flavors such as Peruvian and Indian fare. Visitors can also explore boutique shopping, farmers markets and community events that showcase the area’s local culture.

Outdoor enthusiasts are drawn to nearby destinations like the Noxubee National Wildlife Refuge, which offers hiking trails, wildlife viewing and scenic landscapes just outside the city.

Known as “Mississippi’s College Town,” Starkville has built a reputation for its welcoming atmosphere, particularly during Mississippi State game days, when the campus fills with visitors and alumni. City leaders and residents say the recognition reflects what locals have long known: that Starkville offers a unique blend of small-town warmth and big-city amenities, making it a standout destination in the South.

HORN LAKE – Horn Lake police are searching for two suspects after a man was shot during an assault in a McDonald’s parking lot last month.

According to police, officers responded March 26, 2026, to a report of a suspicious person in the parking lot of the McDonald’s at 4170 Fountain Lane. When officers arrived, they found a male victim lying in the parking lot with a gunshot wound to his upper shoulder.

Emergency medical personnel transported the man to a hospital for treatment, and he was later released.

Investigators said the victim had been jumped by several people in the parking lot. During the confrontation, two people who initially approached the victim pulled out a handgun, and during a brief struggle, one of them fired a shot that struck the man in the shoulder.

Horn Lake investigators said they were able to identify several people involved in the assault.

Police said warrants have been issued for 22-year-old Markevion Williams on charges of aggravated assault with a weapon and felony conspiracy to commit a crime. A warrant also has been issued for 20-year-old Morgan Williams on a charge of felony conspiracy to commit a crime.

Anyone with information about the whereabouts of Markevion Williams or Morgan Williams is asked to contact the Horn Lake Police Department at 662-393-6174.

STARKVILLE — Mississippi State is pointing future and current students to a new university resource to help explore academic programs and select a major.

MSU is introducing Major Maps, a year-by-year roadmap containing information about each undergraduate major at the university. The online tool can help prospective students and their families understand what a major offers and what to expect from each academic pathway toward a bachelor’s degree. The information guide also is useful for career planning as it shows how each major positions graduates for future opportunities.

“Students and families alike are asking thoughtful questions about the value of a degree and how it connects to future opportunities. Major Maps helps answer these questions by presenting clear, consistent information about what students will study, how they can enrich that experience, and where that path can lead after graduation,” said MSU Provost and Executive Vice President David Shaw.

“Major Maps is a practical tool that supports students from the moment they begin exploring Mississippi State through graduation and beyond. By helping students better understand their academic options, stay on track in their programs, and connect their degree to future careers, this resource advances key priorities for how we support students at MSU,” he added.

Available at www.majors.msstate.edu , Major Maps supports several MSU goals, including serving as a strong support system to recruit prospective students to the state’s leading university, improve student retention and further increase employability by helping students better articulate the value of each degree. It also supports academic advising, giving students and advisors a shared, easy-to-read reference outlining important curricular milestones, suggested co-curricular experiences and ways students can stay on track academically.

Shelby Tschume, executive director for strategic initiatives in MSU’s Office of the Provost, said not only future and current students, but a broad variety of users will benefit from the streamlined information presented through Major Maps. From parents and family members to advisors, faculty and external partners, the tool offers clarity and consistency.

“This will be extremely helpful to anyone seeking accurate information about MSU majors, and we have designed this tool to feel welcoming, informative and easy to navigate. We want all our students to feel confident about the majors they are choosing and how they can make the most of their time at the university,” Tschume said. She also expressed appreciation for the collaborative effort among faculty, staff and college leaders in bringing the project to fruition.

Major Exploration Workshops co-hosted by the Career Center and the Center for Advising will assist students who are undecided on a major to compare different programs and learn how various options align with their personal interests, skills and career goals.

Mississippi State University is taking care of what matters. Learn more at www.msstate.edu.
